To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

men with a prostate cancer antigen 2 (PCA3) score ≥100 have a 4- to 6-fold increased risk of prostate cancer (PCa) compared with men with lower PCA3 scores, and that PCA3 is a useful test to rule out PCa in men with a low risk of PCa.
men who present with a PSA score of >10 ng/ml and a high PCA3 score (>100) are at high risk of having a prostate cancer diagnosis.
men presenting to the clinic with elevated PSA scores and high urinary PSA levels have a high risk of having prostate cancer and that this risk is independent of PSA level and age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of prostate cancer.
the use of the prostate cancer antigen 1 and 2, or PSA, as a marker for prostate cancer.
the development of a new method for the diagnosis of prostate cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of prostate cancer antigen 2 is not recommended for use in the screening of prostate cancer in asymptomatic men.
a PSA score of >100 in the absence of any other symptoms or signs of prostate cancer would warrant further investigation.
a PSA score of ≥ 10 ng/ml, with a PSAV score of ≥ 3.0 ng/ml/yr and/or PSA density of > 0.2 ng/ml/cc, is a significant risk factor for prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to understand why some patients develop a particular disease, and what can be done about it.
we have demonstrated the utility of PCA3 in men with a PSA level ≥2.5 ng/mL.

we have demonstrated that the combination of a high urinary prostate cancer antigen (PCA) 3 score (PCA3 >100) and an abnormal digital rectal examination (DRE) is highly predictive of a positive biopsy result, with a positive predictive value (PPV) of 80%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PSA is not a reliable screening tool, and that PSA screening is not associated with a reduction in prostate cancer mortality.
the prostate cancer antigen 2 (PCA3) test can be a helpful adjunct to the PSA test in patients who are being evaluated for prostate cancer.
the PSA test, as it is currently used, is not an effective screening test for prostate cancer.
